concept_html:
Every change to a prompt, model, chunk size or retrieval setting can fix some answers and break others. A regression eval runs one evaluation set on the current version, the baseline, and on the candidate, then decides whether the candidate may ship.

  • Freeze the set and split it. Keep a development set for trying ideas and a test set you only use to decide. Tuning on the test set makes its score optimistic, as with any model (module B11).
  • Compare item by item. Pass rates hide churn. A candidate at 84% against a baseline at 84% can have fixed 20 items and broken 20 others. Count the fixed items (fail to pass) and the broken ones (pass to fail), and read every broken one.
  • Repeat noisy items. Replies vary between calls, so run each item three times and take the majority verdict: it passes when sum(runs) > len(runs) / 2. An item that passes one run in three is unstable. Flag it, whatever the majority says.
  • Write the gate before you run. For example: every critical item passes, at most two items break, and the pass rate drops by no more than two points. Critical items include questions the sources cannot answer, where the only right reply is the refusal.
  • Log the run. Record model, prompt version, eval set version, verdicts per item and token counts in MLflow (module B14) or the run log. A later regression can then be traced to the change that caused it.
fixed = sorted(q for q in baseline if not baseline[q] and candidate[q])
broken = sorted(q for q in baseline if baseline[q] and not candidate[q])

Both runs must cover the same items. A candidate that skipped a hard question would look better than it is, so check the keys match before you compare.

"""Items fixed and broken by the candidate.
Raises:
ValueError: If the two runs cover different items.
"""
if baseline.keys() != candidate.keys():
raise ValueError("baseline and candidate cover different items")
return {
"fixed": sorted(q for q in baseline if not baseline[q] and candidate[q]),
"broken": sorted(q for q in baseline if baseline[q] and not candidate[q]),
}
def release_gate(
baseline: dict[str, bool],
candidate: dict[str, bool],
critical: set[str],
max_broken: int = 2,
max_drop: float = 0.02,
) -> tuple[bool, list[str]]:
"""Decide whether the candidate may ship, with the reasons if not.
Args:
baseline: Pass or fail per item for the current version.
candidate: Pass or fail per item for the new version.
critical: Items that must pass, such as must-refuse questions.
max_broken: Most items allowed to go from pass to fail.
max_drop: Largest allowed fall in pass rate, as a share.
Returns:
True with no reasons, or False with every rule that failed.
"""
changes = compare_runs(baseline, candidate)
reasons = [f"critical:{q}" for q in sorted(critical) if not candidate[q]]
if len(changes["broken"]) > max_broken:
reasons.append("too_many_broken")
drop = sum(baseline.values()) / len(baseline) - sum(candidate.values()) / len(candidate)
if drop > max_drop:
reasons.append("pass_rate_drop")
return not reasons, reasons

title: Regression evals and release gates for prompt changes
why_html: A prompt rewrite raised the pass rate from 86% to 89%, and it shipped. A week later, clients received confident answers about wave W15, which had not started: the new prompt had stopped refusing questions the sources could not answer. Three critical "must refuse" items had broken, hidden inside a higher average. A gate that required every critical item to pass would have blocked the release.
